title: IRS Officer Ekta Vishnoi Wins Three Golds at World Masters Powerlifting in Nevada
excerpt: The Joint Secretary in the Department of Biotechnology lifted 362.5 kg to top the M2 57 kg category ahead of Canada and Japan — coached by video call after her coach's US visa was denied.
body:
• IRS officer Ekta Vishnoi won three gold medals at the World Masters Classic and Equipped Powerlifting Championships in Nevada, lifting a combined 362.5 kg in the M2 (50-59 years), 57 kg category.
  • Her lifts — 130 kg squat, 72.5 kg bench press and 160 kg deadlift — put her ahead of the Canadian lifter on 330 kg and the Japanese lifter on 325 kg, making her the first Indian woman to win Masters-2 gold at the championship.
  • Her coach, Sunil Kumar, was denied a US visa before the event; Vishnoi competed using his guidance by video call, with on-ground support from team official Binu Ibrahim.
  • Vishnoi, a Joint Secretary in the Department of Biotechnology who took up powerlifting at 45, balances a senior civil-service post with training under coach Sunil at Netaji Gym in New Delhi.

Indian Revenue Service officer Ekta Vishnoi has won three gold medals at the World Masters Classic and Equipped Powerlifting Championships in Nevada, lifting a combined 362.5 kg to become the first Indian female powerlifter to win gold in the Masters-2 category of the championship, according to PTI reporting.

Vishnoi, presently serving as Joint Secretary in the Government of India's Department of Biotechnology, topped the M2 (50-59 years), 57 kg category in a field that included competitors from Canada and Japan.

The lifts that won it

Vishnoi recorded 130 kg in the squat, 72.5 kg in the bench press and 160 kg in the deadlift, for a 362.5 kg total. The Canadian competitor finished second on 330 kg and the Japanese lifter third on 325 kg — margins of 32.5 kg and 37.5 kg. According to IANS, the gold was effectively sealed early: by the end of the squat, Vishnoi had built a 20 kg lead over her closest rival, held it through the bench press, and closed the contest with a successful opening deadlift of 150 kg before extending her total.

"Our strategy was crystal clear. By the conclusion of the squat event, we had already built a decisive 20 kg lead over our closest rival. Ekta successfully maintained this crucial lead through the bench press event. Finally, with a successful opening deadlift of 150 kg, Ekta sealed the historic gold medal for India."

— Sunil Kumar, coach

Coached by video call

The campaign nearly lost its architect before it began. Ahead of the tournament, coach Sunil Kumar's US visa was denied. Vishnoi adapted, taking his guidance by video call during the competition, with on-ground support from team official Binu Ibrahim, and executed the planned attempt selection without him in the venue. Kumar said the team adopted a scientific, result-oriented approach to attempt selection. Her partner, Ajay Tomar, said the preparation had a single focus: "Prior to the World Championship, our preparation was absolute and thorough. We shared a single-minded goal: to win the gold medal for our motherland, India."

A second career begun at 45

Vishnoi trains under Kumar at the Netaji Gym in New Delhi while holding a Joint Secretary-level post in the Department of Biotechnology — a senior administrative role in India's biotechnology policy apparatus. She took up powerlifting at 45, and within seven years has progressed from a beginner to a world Masters champion in her age and weight class, a trajectory that has made her a recurring subject of profiles of mid-career Indian civil servants in elite sport. Her triple gold in Nevada is the strongest result of that run: three gold medals at a single world championship, in both classic and equipped competition, against the leading Masters lifters from Canada and Japan.

Why the result matters

Masters powerlifting rarely draws mainstream attention in India, and Indian women have had few headline results in the sport at world level. Vishnoi's win is a first in her category for an Indian woman, achieved in the United States against a field drawn from established powerlifting nations. It also extends a pattern Indian sports administrators have been keen to highlight: senior civil servants competing internationally while in service, with the Department of Biotechnology's own leadership having previously felicitated her for an earlier world championship silver. For younger Indian lifters — and for women considering strength sports later in life — a 362.5 kg total at a world championship, built on a start at 45, is now the reference point.
